# Week 1 - Day 1 - Fundamentals - Why automation, why Playwright

Software testing means checking that an application works the way it should. This lesson explains
what testing is, how automated testing differs from testing by hand, and why this course uses a
tool called Playwright.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | An orientation to test automation, with one guided look at the Playwright website. |
| **Goals** | Explain what automation cannot do, why teams choose Playwright over Selenium, and where automation effort is spent. |
| **Prerequisites** | No prior knowledge is required. This is the first lesson in the course. |
| **Key takeaway** | Automation does not find defects. It reports whether each check passed or failed. |

## What software testing is

An **application** is a program that people use, such as a banking website or a shopping app.
Before an application is released, someone must check that it works. That work is called
**software testing**.

A tester works from a **test case**: a list of steps, and the result those steps should produce.
The result the steps should produce is the **expected result**. The result you see when you follow
the steps is the **actual result**. When the two are different, the tester has found a **bug**,
which is also called a **defect**.

| Part of a test case | Example |
|---|---|
| Steps | Open the login page, enter a valid email and password, and select **Login**. |
| Expected result | The account dashboard opens. |
| Actual result | An error message appears. |
| Outcome | The actual result is different from the expected result, so this is a bug. |

## Manual testing and automated testing

In **manual testing**, a person follows the steps of a test case and decides whether the result
is correct.

In **automated testing**, a program follows the same steps. A program that runs a test is called a
**test script**, or a test for short. You write the script once, and it can then run the test as
often as you need.

| | Manual testing | Automated testing |
|---|---|---|
| Who follows the steps | A person | A test script |
| Who decides whether the result is correct | The person, using their judgment | The script only compares the actual result with the expected result it was given. |
| Can it notice a problem that nobody planned to check? | Yes. A person can see that something looks wrong. | No. It checks only what it was told to check. |
| Best suited to | Exploring a new feature for the first time | Repeating the same checks many times, for example every night |
| Cost of each run | High, because it uses a person's time | Very low, once the script is written |

This leads to the most important idea in this lesson. **Automation does not find bugs.** It
reports whether each check **passed** or **failed**. When a check fails, a person investigates and
decides whether the failure is a bug.

## What you need before you automate a test

You need two things before you can automate a test:

1. **A known expected result.** You must know what the correct result looks like. Otherwise, the
   script has nothing to compare the actual result with.
2. **A way to find the element.** An **element** is one item on a web page, such as a button, a
   text field, or a link. Testers also call it an **object**. The script must be able to find the
   element reliably every time, so that it can click it, type into it, or read it.

If either one is missing, the test cannot be automated. This is why some testing, such as exploring
a new feature without a fixed goal, stays manual.

## What Playwright is

**Playwright** is a free, open-source tool, made by Microsoft, for the automated testing of web
applications. **Open-source** means that anyone can read and use its code.

Playwright controls a **web browser**, the program you use to visit websites, in the same way a
person does. It opens pages, clicks buttons, and types text. Because it uses the application the way
a user does, from the first step of a task to the last, Playwright is called an **end-to-end
testing** tool. An end-to-end test checks a complete task, such as signing in and viewing an
account balance.

Playwright works with the three main browser engines. A **browser engine** is the part of a browser
that displays web pages.

| Engine | Used by |
|---|---|
| Chromium | Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge |
| Firefox | Mozilla Firefox |
| WebKit | Apple Safari |

You write Playwright tests in a programming language. This course uses **TypeScript**, and the
TypeScript lessons begin in [Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1). Playwright also supports
JavaScript, Python, Java, and C#.

## Why teams choose Playwright

Before Playwright, many teams used **Selenium**, an older testing tool that is still widely used.
With Selenium, teams usually add several other tools to build a complete setup. Playwright includes
those tools itself:

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| Automatic waiting | A web page can take a moment to load. Playwright waits for each element to be ready before it clicks or types, so you do not need to add waits yourself. |
| Assertions | An **assertion** is a check that compares the actual result with the expected result. Playwright includes its own assertions. |
| Test runner | A **test runner** is the program that starts your tests and reports which passed and which failed. Playwright includes one. |
| Screenshots and video | When a test fails, Playwright can save screenshots and a video, so that you can see what happened. |
| Codegen | **Codegen** records your clicks in a browser and writes the matching test code. You use it in [Day 4 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d4/p2). |

Selenium remains a good choice for many teams. Playwright is newer, and it was designed to include
the tools that teams had to add to Selenium separately.

## Other kinds of testing tools

Playwright tests applications through a web browser. Other kinds of testing need other tools. Each
kind of testing is also called a testing **vertical**.

| Kind of testing | What it checks | Example tools |
|---|---|---|
| Web interface (UI) | The application in a browser, the way a user sees it | Playwright, Selenium, Cypress |
| API | The requests and responses that programs exchange, without a browser. An **API** is the way one program asks another for data. | Postman, REST Assured, Playwright |
| Performance | How the application behaves when many people use it at the same time | JMeter, k6, Gatling |
| Mobile apps | Apps that people install on a phone | Appium |

Playwright can make a desktop browser imitate a phone screen. This is called **mobile emulation**.
It is useful for testing websites on phone-sized screens, but it does not test apps that are
installed on a phone. For those, testers use a mobile testing tool such as Appium.

## Where the effort goes

Learning a testing tool is only part of the work. On a typical project, the effort divides roughly
like this:

| Share of the effort | Spent on |
|---|---|
| About half | Learning the application: what it does, how people use it, and what the correct result is for each task |
| About half | Three skills together: the programming language, finding elements reliably, and organizing the steps and checks of each test |

Knowing the application matters as much as knowing the tool.

## Explore the Playwright website

Open a new browser tab and follow these steps:

1. Go to **https://playwright.dev**.
2. Read the short description at the top of the home page, and the three features listed below it.
3. Select **Docs**, then **Writing tests**, and read the page quickly. The code on that page makes
   more sense after [Day 5 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2), where you write your first test.
4. Write down one thing on the site that this lesson did not mention. You need it for
   [Practice](/learn/w1/d1/p4).
An automated test script runs 500 checks every night, and all of them pass. What does this tell you?

options: The application has no bugs in the areas that the checks cover.
The 500 checks that a person wrote produced their expected results.
No new bugs have appeared in the application since the last run.
checkpoint.explanation: Automation does not find bugs. Each check compares the actual result with an expected result that a person wrote in advance. A problem that nobody wrote a check for still passes, which is why people continue to test by hand as well.

blocks.text: According to this lesson, which two things do you need before you can automate a test?

options: A test runner, a report, and a tool that records video
A known expected result and a way to find the element
A fast computer and a colleague to review your script
checkpoint.explanation: Without a known expected result, the script has nothing to compare the actual result with. Without a reliable way to find the element, the script cannot click it, type into it, or read it. If either one is missing, the test stays manual.

blocks.text: Your manager asks you to automate tests for the company's Android app, which people install on their phones. Is Playwright the right tool?

options: Yes, because mobile support is one of the features Playwright lists.
No. Playwright imitates phone screens in a browser and cannot test installed apps.
Yes, but only on an emulator on your computer, not on a real phone.
checkpoint.explanation: Playwright's mobile support is mobile emulation: a desktop browser imitates a phone screen. This is useful for testing websites on phone-sized screens. An app installed on a phone needs a mobile testing tool such as Appium.

blocks.text:
- **Software testing** checks that an application works as expected. A bug is a difference between the expected result and the actual result.
- **Automation does not find bugs.** It reports whether each check passed or failed, and a person decides what a failure means.
- Before you automate a test, you need a known expected result and a way to find the element.
- **Playwright** is a free, open-source tool that tests web applications through a browser, from the first step of a task to the last.
- About half of the effort on a project goes into learning the application. The other half goes into the language, finding elements, and organizing each test.

## What's next

Continue to [Practice](/learn/w1/d1/p4) for three short problems. In
[Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2), you set up your computer so that you can write and run
tests.

Three reflection and research problems, in the same three tiers as every practice day.

## When you're done

You've now got the "why" — why teams automate, why Playwright specifically, and where the
effort really goes. [Day 2](/learn/w1/d2/p2) starts turning that into a working environment
on your machine.

problems.statement:
**What to do.** Pick one manual test you've personally run by hand (in any app, past job, or
this course's banking app if you've poked at it already). Write two sentences: could
Playwright automate it, and what *object* would you need to identify on the page to do so?

**How you'll know it worked.** You named a concrete object (a button, a field, a label) —
not just "the login page" in the abstract. If you can't name one, that's worth noticing: it
might mean the test isn't automatable yet, per today's thumb rule.
problems.stub:
// Your turn — jot your answer here as a comment, or a console.log if you want
// to see it printed. There's no code to run today, only thinking to do.
problems.solution:
**A model answer — yours will name a different test, and that is the point.**

> *Manual test:* logging in to the banking app with a valid email and password and checking the dashboard appears.
>
> *Could Playwright automate it?* Yes. It has a known expected result (the dashboard loads and shows my name) and every step acts on something identifiable on the page.
>
> *The object I would need to identify:* the **Login button** — specifically `getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' })`. I would also need the two placeholder-labeled inputs, `Enter Email` and `Enter Password`.

**What makes an answer good here** is naming a concrete control, such as a button, a field or a label, rather than "the login page". If you could not name one, that is the honest signal this lesson was pointing at: a step no human can describe as *"click this specific thing"* is a step automation cannot perform either.

A weak answer says "automate the login page". A strong one says "click the button whose accessible name is Login".

problems.statement:
**What to do.** Open https://playwright.dev again and find **three features** it mentions
that this lesson didn't cover. For each one, write one sentence on what it's for.

**How you'll know it worked.** Three genuinely different features (not three rewordings of
"auto-wait"), each with a one-line explanation in your own words.

> **Hint** — check the homepage feature grid, the sidebar under "Guides", and the "Tools"
> section if the site has one. Codegen and the Inspector don't count — those are already in
> today's lesson.
problems.stub:
// Your turn — jot your answer here as a comment, or a console.log if you want
// to see it printed. There's no code to run today, only thinking to do.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.** Three features the lesson did not cover, taken from the feature grid, the Guides sidebar, and the Tools menu on [playwright.dev](https://playwright.dev):

1. **Trace Viewer** — records a run as a time-traveling trace: DOM snapshot, network, console and the action log for every step. It is how you debug a failure that only happens in CI, after the fact.
2. **Test Retries** — re-runs a failed test a configured number of times before reporting it failed, so a genuinely flaky test is visible as flaky rather than as a hard failure. You meet this properly in Week 3.
3. **API Testing** — Playwright can send HTTP requests directly through `request`, with no browser at all, which is how you set up state quickly instead of clicking through the UI to reach it.

Other good picks: **Component testing**, **Visual comparisons**, **Mobile emulation**, **Codegen**, **UI Mode**, **Parallelism and sharding**.

**What makes an answer good** is that the three are genuinely different capabilities, each in your own words. Three rewordings of auto-waiting is one feature, not three.

problems.statement:
**What to do.** Pick one testing vertical from today's table that *isn't* UI (API,
performance, or mobile). Imagine a single scenario in that vertical — e.g. "load-test the
login endpoint with 100 concurrent users", or "check the checkout API returns a 200 with a
valid order id". Using today's effort table, write down roughly where the automation effort
would go for that scenario: how much is application knowledge, how much is language, how
much is object identification (or its equivalent — e.g. "the right endpoint and payload"),
and how much is logic.

**How you'll know it worked.** You've named a specific tool from today's vertical table for
that scenario, and your effort breakdown is specific to *that* scenario rather than a
restatement of the general table.
problems.stub:
// Your turn — jot your answer here as a comment, or a console.log if you want
// to see it printed. There's no code to run today, only thinking to do.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.** Taking *"check the checkout API returns a 200 with a valid order id"*:

> **Application knowledge — the majority of the effort.** Which endpoint is actually called at checkout, what a valid request body looks like, which fields are mandatory, what authentication it needs, what "a valid order id" means (format? persisted where?), and what the API does on a *failed* payment. None of this is in any tool's documentation. You get it from the team, the spec, and from watching the real thing.
>
> **Tooling and language — a small slice.** `request.post(url, { data })`, read `response.status()`, parse the JSON, assert on the id. An afternoon with the docs.
>
> **Environment and data — the part that is always underestimated.** A test account that can actually check out, a product that is in stock, a payment method that works in the test environment, and a way to avoid leaving real orders behind on every run.

**The point of the exercise** is the shape of the split: the tool is the small part. This is exactly the thumb rule from the lesson — your core business is the application, not the library. A scenario you cannot describe precisely in English is not one you can automate in any language.
